title: ADIB adds 200,000 customers and a first-of-its-kind open finance licence as nine-month profit climbs to AED 6.4 billion
snippet: Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank has reported a 6 per cent rise in profit before tax to AED 6.4 billion for the first nine months of 2026, with customer financing up a quarter, deposits past AED 250 billion and a non-performing asset ratio at a record low. Behind the headline numbers sits a digital story: the UAE’s first bank licensed as an Open Finance Provider, a newly appointed Chief AI Officer and onboarding journeys cut from days to minutes. The post ADIB adds 200,000 customers and a first-of-its-kind open finance licence as nine-month profit climbs to AED 6.4 billion appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The numbers

ADIB’s nine-month results, published today, show a bank growing on every line that matters. Revenue reached AED 9.7 billion, up 6 per cent year on year, with funded income rising 11 per cent to AED 6.1 billion as financing volumes expanded across both retail and wholesale banking. Non-funded income held broadly flat at AED 3.6 billion, but the direction of travel inside that figure is instructive: net fee and commission income hit AED 591 million in the third quarter, up 11 per cent on the previous quarter and 9 per cent on the year, lifted by card income and processing fees.

Profit after tax for the period was AED 5.6 billion, up 6 per cent, delivering a return on equity of 28 per cent, which the bank describes as industry-leading. Earnings per share rose 5 per cent to AED 1.38.

The balance sheet grew faster than the income statement. Total assets climbed 18 per cent to AED 318 billion. Gross customer financing rose 25 per cent year on year, an increase of AED 43 billion over twelve months, to AED 218 billion. Retail financing was up 21 per cent to AED 109 billion and wholesale financing up 29 per cent to AED 86 billion, with financing to government-related entities now accounting for 26 per cent of the book. Customer deposits grew 17 per cent to AED 259 billion, and current and savings accounts still make up 60 per cent of that total, one of the highest CASA ratios in the sector.

Growth without the credit cost

What distinguishes this set of results from the usual Gulf growth story is that asset quality improved while the book expanded. Impairment charges fell 12 per cent to AED 451 million, putting the cost of risk at 30 basis points. Non-performing financing dropped to AED 4.4 billion from AED 5.7 billion a year earlier, taking the non-performing asset ratio to 2.0 per cent, the lowest in the bank’s history. Provision coverage excluding collateral rose to 114.3 per cent from 89.3 per cent.

Costs rose 9 per cent to AED 2.8 billion, which ADIB attributes to investment in people, technology and business capabilities. The cost-to-income ratio sits at 29.1 per cent, up 88 basis points on the year but still lean by regional standards.

Capital is the one area where the numbers have moved the other way. The Common Equity Tier 1 ratio stood at 12.4 per cent at the end of September, down 64 basis points year on year, as risk-weighted assets grew 15 per cent. The bank’s AED 1.75 billion rights issue is designed to address exactly that, rebuilding headroom for the next phase of growth under its Vision 2035 strategy.

The fintech story underneath

For readers of this title, the more interesting disclosures are in the strategic update rather than the income statement.

ADIB has become the first bank in the UAE licensed to operate as an Open Finance Provider under the Central Bank’s Open Finance regulation, known as AlTareq. The third-party provider licence lets ADIB aggregate customer-permissioned account data from other banks and present it in a single interface, a role that until now has largely been the preserve of fintechs rather than incumbents. It is a notable move: a Sharia-compliant bank positioning itself as the aggregator rather than the aggregated.

The bank has also appointed a dedicated Chief AI Officer, tasked with scaling AI use cases across customer experience, operations and internal processes. Its upgraded digital onboarding for home finance approval and card journeys now lets both existing and new customers apply for a home finance approval in principle, or gain instant access to a card, through a fully digital straight-through process, with onboarding times reduced from days to minutes.

Physical distribution has not been abandoned, but it has been redesigned. Following the opening of its universal branch at Dubai Hills Mall, ADIB has opened an AI-enabled digital branch in Al Ain, combining self-service terminals, kiosks and smart tellers with in-person support.

On the product side, the bank launched ADIB Arrive, a proposition for customers relocating to the UAE that bundles pre-arrival onboarding, salary-transfer rewards and preferential banking benefits, and added co-branded cards with Marriott Bonvoy and with Aldar, the latter rewarding spend across the developer’s residential, retail, education, hospitality and leisure ecosystem.

The result of all this activity is a customer base growing by more than 200,000 in nine months. On the sustainability side, ADIB has mobilised AED 23.3 billion in sustainable finance to date against a target of AED 60 billion by 2030.

What the leadership said

Mohamed Abdelbary, group chief executive officer at ADIB

Chairman H.E. Jawaan Awaidah Al Khaili framed the quarter as validation of the bank’s long-term plan: “ADIB’s continued growth reflects the strength of our franchise and the trust of our customers, with strong financing momentum, an expanding customer base and strong asset quality positioning the Bank well for the next phase of growth under Vision 2035.”

Group Chief Executive Officer Mohamed Abdelbary pointed to the breadth of the growth: “Our performance reflects the broad-based growth across ADIB, with strong profitability, continued customer and financing growth, and robust asset quality. Supported by the strength of our franchise and a healthy pipeline across retail and wholesale banking, we are well positioned to sustain this momentum as we execute Vision 2035.”

The view from The Fintech Times

Islamic banks in the Gulf have historically been strong on balance sheet and cautious on technology. ADIB’s nine-month update suggests that framing is out of date. A 25 per cent increase in financing paired with a falling NPA ratio is a credit story, but a 200,000-customer intake, an open finance aggregator licence and a Chief AI Officer are a fintech story, and the two are now being told from the same results deck.

The open finance licence is the one to watch. The UAE’s AlTareq framework is among the most ambitious open finance regimes anywhere, extending beyond payments and current accounts into insurance, investments and lending. An incumbent that chooses to be a data consumer as well as a data provider is betting that it can build the customer interface of the future faster than the fintechs can build the balance sheet. The next few quarters will show whether that bet is paying off in fee income as well as in customer numbers.

ADIB is headquartered in Abu Dhabi, listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, and operates in Egypt, Iraq, the United Kingdom and Qatar alongside its UAE network.

title: How Singapore Became and Remains a Fintech Powerhouse
snippet: Singapore is fast becoming a global fintech powerhouse. Georgia Hanias looks at the startups, investment, tax advantages and innovation driving its success. The post How Singapore Became and Remains a Fintech Powerhouse appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
What does it take to become a leading fintech hub? Having lived in London for decades and had the good fortune to join the city’s ecosystem in its early years as a founding team member of Innovate Finance – the world’s first truly successful trade body for the industry – I can recite the key ingredients by heart: favourable regulation, access to talent, access to investment, and favourable time zones.

I have heard the saying ‘London is Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Washington all wrapped into one’ many times, and I like it a lot. It perfectly reflects my own lived experience supporting the countless companies I have worked with over the years. In London, you can literally meet amazingly talented tech people speaking with the world’s biggest financial institutions at a regulatory sandbox hosted by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). All in a single day.

And let’s not forget the press – all the world’s top media outlets are in London. The city offers access to the best writers, who seamlessly sell these stories to a population that adopts new fintech at a speed many other nations can’t match. No wonder this great megacity is home to more fintech unicorns than any other nation on earth, bar the US and China – the world’s two biggest economies.

Fourteen years since the launch of Innovate Finance and its support for many of the most successful fintechs in the world – from Revolut and Wise to Klarna and Monzo – there is a lot that the UK can be proud of. But what is intriguing me more these days is what’s happening on the other side of the world.

Shifting focus to the East

Folks, I have been blown away by what I am seeing in Singapore, and I’ve been trying to figure out its secret sauce. The country’s fintech sector has raised over $12.5billion over the last five years. It is home to more than 1,600 registered fintech firms, accounting for nearly 60 per cent of ASEAN’s fintech funding and more than half of the region’s deals. How can a place that is literally smaller in both population and landmass than London become such an epicentre for financial innovation?

Beyond Silicon Valley – homegrown success

To answer this question, you only have to look at the scaling journey of entrepreneurs like Rahul Shinghal, CEO and co-founder of Tazapay for some clues. His Singaporean home grown B2B cross border payment company was established just six years ago and was recently acquired by Circle in a deal that some media reports have valued at $400million.

During a panel hosted at INSEAD’s Singaporean campus, he told an audience of students that Singapore is a great place to scale up a fintech company as long as you have a market fit for your business. Forget the UK or San Francisco. Everything else you need to grow is accessible from here.

Singapore’s secret sauce is no big secret

He’s right. Like London, Singapore has got the favourable regulator, the talent and the investment pool – not to mention its proximity to the biggest populations in the world to convert as fintech users. All the international press also have correspondents based here – and are ready to share the biggest advancements coming out of this city-state.

But another major draw which is a true game changer is its tax regime. With a corporate tax rate of 17 per cent no dividend or capital gains taxes and a personal income tax capped at 24 per cent, Singapore is miles ahead of the UK when it comes to a business friendly environment and undoubtedly why so many companies have set up here and are thriving.

The proof of this approach is in its results: the list of Singaporean headquartered companies taking both local as well as global market share by storm are impressive in their calibre and quality.

Best of breed: fintech giants taking the world by storm

Take Airwallex, the global platform that helps businesses manage cross-border payments and multi-currency accounts. At this year’s Formula 1 in Singapore, you could see their logo everywhere as it became the McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team’s first official AI finance partner. The company has been valued at US$11billion following a US$320million Series H funding round in June this year.

Another big one is Grab – South East Asia’s multibillion dollar ‘everyday, everything’ super app. Most visitors of Singapore will refer to it as an uber equivalent, but it is so much more than that. So far, I have used the app to hail a cab, buy travel insurance, rent a bike, apply for a credit card, book a restaurant table, and pay the bill. I even used it to open an account with GXS, a brilliant local digital bank. Thanks to Singpass –Singapore’s life-changing digital identity infrastructure stored on my mobile phone — the onboarding and KYC process was completely seamless.

The list of fintech superstars goes on and includes Nium, a unicorn which builds cross-border payment infrastructure for businesses, and Coda Payments, a global leader in digital content monetisation and distribution, which made headlines in Europe last year when it bought prepaid payments platform Recharge, in what was hailed as largest fintech acquisition in Dutch history. There’s also companies like ShopBack – the free cashback and rewards platform and Advance Intelligence Group, which are leading the charge in the BNPL and enterprise software solution space.

Built on efficiency and frictionless innovation

Lee Kuan Yew, the founding Prime Minister of Singapore attributed its success to the rejection of “economic populism” and that “foreign investments are necessary; we must make Singapore attractive to investors”.

The country has succeeded in its mission, and like the catch phrase for my local GXS bank, its continual backing of innovation “breaks boundaries, not sweat!”

But for me, what makes this place really tick is how efficient it is – everything works brilliantly – and frictionlessly. And may I add – the MRT tube station is phenomenal and so well priced at less than £2 for a return ticket. Of course, like many great cities, Singapore is expensive, but you feel that your tax dollars are being put to good use.

While London remains a thriving fintech hub and will always feel like home, I can’t help but be blown away by the tenacity and scale of this nation’s ecosystem. I am looking forward to meeting more founders and hearing from many of the ecosystem’s biggest stars at this year’s Singapore Fintech Festival and finding out where the next wave of innovation will take us.

title: StraitsX and Visa to Extend Stablecoin Card Issuing to 100+ Markets
snippet: StraitsX will use Visa's network to scale stablecoin-backed card programmes globally, building on US$6bn in annualised Asian card volume. The post StraitsX and Visa to Extend Stablecoin Card Issuing to 100+ Markets appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
StraitsX, the Singapore-based stablecoin infrastructure provider licensed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), has announced a partnership with Visa to expand its stablecoin-backed card issuing capabilities to more than 100 markets globally. The deal, disclosed on 15 October 2026, is framed as the next stage in StraitsX’s growth after establishing a significant card business across Asia.

The company reported annualised gross transaction volume of more than US$6 billion across its stablecoin-backed card programmes in Asia, a figure that gives the partnership a credible commercial foundation. The expanded capability is designed for fintechs, Digital Payment Token (DPT) service providers and wallet operators that want to issue cards connected to stablecoin balances and digital asset payment flows, while consumers and merchants continue to use the standard Visa acceptance network. The announcement noted that the expansion remains subject to applicable regulatory, compliance and Visa requirements.

Tianwei Liu, chief executive and co-founder of StraitsX, said the growth of stablecoin-backed cards in Asia had demonstrated a practical path from settlement-layer use case to everyday payments. “Expanding our issuing capabilities globally allows us to bring the same infrastructure to businesses looking to build and scale card programs across markets,” he said. Rubail Birwadker, Global Head of Growth Products and Partnerships at Visa, described the collaboration as connecting stablecoin payment flows to the scale and reliability of Visa’s global network.

Why card issuing matters for stablecoin infrastructure

The structural significance of this deal lies in the distribution model. Stablecoin-to-card bridging is one of the few mechanisms through which dollar or Singapore-dollar denominated stablecoins can be used at the point of sale without requiring merchant adoption of new payment rails. By sitting inside the Visa acceptance network, StraitsX can offer its fintech and DPT-service-provider clients access to tens of millions of merchant locations while retaining stablecoin balances and settlement on its own infrastructure layer.

StraitsX issues the XUSD and XSGD stablecoins and holds a Major Payment Institution licence from MAS. That regulatory standing matters in the current environment. Several stablecoin issuers are navigating new licensing frameworks across key markets: MiCA in the European Union came into force for electronic money tokens earlier this year, and regulators in the Gulf, including the UAE’s VARA and ADGM, have established their own stablecoin regimes. Any expansion into those jurisdictions will require StraitsX to satisfy local licensing requirements before card programmes can be launched, which is presumably the significance of the “applicable regulatory approvals” caveat in the release.

Market context and competitive positioning

StraitsX is not alone in pursuing this model. Several other infrastructure providers are working to connect stablecoin balances to card networks, including firms operating in the US, Europe and South-East Asia. Visa itself has been active in this space for several years, having previously expanded its stablecoin settlement pilots and partnered with other stablecoin issuers. The competitive question for StraitsX is whether its Asia-rooted regulatory track record and existing GTV volume give it a differentiated position in signing fintech clients outside that home region.

The release also flagged that the collaboration would account for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing risk arising from stablecoin-card integration, a non-trivial operational consideration given the cross-border nature of the product and the varied AML frameworks across the 100-plus target markets.

The next concrete milestones to watch are the specific non-Asian markets where card programmes go live, any further stablecoin licences StraitsX acquires outside Singapore, and whether the US$6 billion annualised GTV figure grows as global issuance comes online.

title: Pliant Wins FCA EMI Licence to Serve UK B2B Payments Market Directly
snippet: The Berlin-based B2B payments platform can now issue payment products in the UK through its own regulated entity, Pliant Payments Limited. The post Pliant Wins FCA EMI Licence to Serve UK B2B Payments Market Directly appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Pliant, the Berlin-headquartered modular B2B payments platform, has received full authorisation from the Financial Conduct Authority as an Electronic Money Institution, granting its UK subsidiary, Pliant Payments Limited, the standing to issue payment products and serve customers directly under a locally regulated entity. The authorisation was announced on 14 October 2026.

Malte Rau, CEO and co-founder of Pliant

The milestone closes a structural gap in Pliant’s UK market position. The company had previously operated in the UK through its Finnish subsidiary, a common bridging arrangement among European fintechs that hold an EU e-money licence but have not yet secured a post-Brexit UK authorisation of their own. That arrangement provides market access but limits commercial independence: contractual relationships, safeguarding obligations and product structuring are all routed through an entity incorporated in a different jurisdiction, which can slow product iteration and add friction for regulated UK counterparties such as banks and public-sector bodies.

Malte Rau, chief executive and co-founder of Pliant, said: “This authorisation gives us greater independence and flexibility to serve UK customers directly. It also puts us in a stronger position to bring our technology to more businesses, financial institutions and public-sector organisations as we continue to expand our capabilities and reach.”

What the licence unlocks

As an authorised EMI, Pliant Payments Limited can issue e-money, hold client funds under the FCA’s safeguarding regime, and build payment programmes for corporate customers without relying on a third-party licensed entity in the UK. For a platform that positions itself as infrastructure for fintechs, software platforms and banks building their own commercial card and payment offerings, holding a UK licence is a commercial pre-condition rather than a regulatory nicety. Regulated financial institutions conducting due diligence on a vendor typically require the vendor to carry its own local licence rather than passport from elsewhere.

Pliant’s broader product stack covers commercial card issuing, payment accounts, foreign exchange and spend management. The company is a principal member of both Visa and Mastercard and currently issues commercial cards in 13 currencies across 32 countries. It also positions its API-first infrastructure as compatible with AI agent use cases, with permissions and auditability built in at the platform level.

Regulatory and competitive context

The FCA’s EMI authorisation process has become more demanding since the UK diverged from EU payments regulation after Brexit. Applicants face scrutiny of customer onboarding procedures, risk management frameworks, safeguarding arrangements and financial controls, a process Pliant described as extensive. The pace of approvals has also been a constraint for the market: several European fintechs have waited considerably longer than expected for UK licences, creating a bottleneck that has shaped how the sector structures its UK go-to-market strategies.

Pliant now sits alongside a growing cohort of European B2B payments and commercial card providers that have secured their own FCA EMI status, including firms competing in the corporate spend management and banking-as-a-service segments. The UK commercial payments market continues to attract entrants given the scale of business card spend and the fragmentation of legacy corporate banking infrastructure, but the segment is increasingly crowded. Pliant’s differentiation case rests on its modular, API-first architecture and its stated capacity to support complex, multi-currency payment workflows for enterprise and AI-native technology clients.

The next indicators to watch will be the pace of new UK client signings, any expansion of the public-sector partnerships referenced in the announcement, and whether Pliant pursues additional UK regulatory permissions beyond the base EMI authorisation.

title: Euronet, Fireblocks pursue stablecoin cards
snippet: The companies are extending their partnership to provide financial firms with the infrastructure needed to issue stablecoin-funded cards.

The companies are extending their partnership to provide financial firms with the infrastructure needed to issue stablecoin-funded cards.

Dive Brief:

Euronet, the international payments infrastructure provider, and Fireblocks, the digital asset infrastructure company, are collaborating to enable banks, fintech and other financial firms to create their own stablecoin-funded card offerings, Euronet said in a press release.

Financial firms that use Euronet’s Ren and CoreCard issuing services can now access Fireblock’s embedded wallet infrastructure that holds and transfers stablecoins, the Oct. 19 release said. 

The companies are providing the service as a white-label offering that financial firms can integrate into their own banking and mobile wallet apps, per the release.

Dive Insight:

Through the partnership, Euronet and Fireblocks aim to bring stablecoin card programs into new markets and bridge the gap between digital assets and traditional card payments, the release said. The two previously partnered last year to offer settlement and pre-funding services for cross-border payments, per the release. 

“A decade ago, stablecoins were just a trader’s tool to exit Bitcoin,” Fireblock’s chief payments and network officer, Ran Goldi, said in a release. “Today, combined with global cards, they are the ideal off-ramp for digital assets.”

Along with Euronet and Fireblocks, other major payments players, including card network Visa and processor Fiserv, as well as startups, are also eyeing the stablecoin market. 

Earlier this month, MassPay, the Las Vegas-based direct payments company, said it teamed up with Block’s Cash App to provide a real-time payments service to those digital wallet account holders. 

In a September interview, MassPay CEO Ran Grushkowsky said the company, which uses digital asset technology to provide payments to gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers, has seen “growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation.”

Meanwhile, Rain, the stablecoin infrastructure company, joined money transfer company Western Union’s digital asset network last year and locked arms with its rival MoneyGram in September. Rain enables corporate clients to integrate its digital asset technology into their architecture. 

As startups vie for digital asset clientele, established payments providers have been racing to integrate stablecoins into traditional finance. 

In July, a consortium of about 140 companies, including payments giants like Visa and digital payments provider Stripe, convened to launch the Open USD stablecoin. 

The following month, Visa and its smaller competitor Mastercard joined forces with Circle Internet Group to support Arc, an initiative that seeks to underpin stablecoin transactions in financial markets, real-time payments and agentic commerce.

Though some newcomers and established payments companies alike are working to bring stablecoins into the mainstream financial system, others are wary of embracing the technology. 

A Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank survey of 148 companies in its district found that financial firms aren’t embracing stablecoins, because of their satisfaction with current payment methods; little demand from customers; and a lack of familiarity with the digital asset class.

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

title: Amex Publishes Intent-Authentication Framework for AI Agent Payments
snippet: American Express has detailed how it will capture and authenticate customer instructions to AI agents before a payment is made, shifting liability to intent records. The post Amex Publishes Intent-Authentication Framework for AI Agent Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
American Express published its Intent Intelligence framework on 13 October, setting out the technical specification for recording, authenticating and transmitting what a customer instructed an AI agent to purchase before any charge is processed. The move makes Amex the first major card network to publish detailed plumbing for agentic commerce, and it has direct implications for how liability will be allocated across the payments stack as autonomous purchasing agents proliferate.

How the framework works

Hannah Bozian, VP of agentic partnerships and strategy at AMEX

The architecture centres on a Create Intent API that captures a customer’s instructions and constraints, covering the merchant, a maximum budget and other preferences. The customer then authenticates and signs off on what the agent recorded. Amex issues an Intent ID and a Proof of Intent Token encoding those high-level constraints. The agent exchanges the token for a scoped payment credential used at checkout in place of the actual card number, and the Intent ID and token travel with the transaction through authorisation, fraud decisioning and any subsequent dispute process.

Hannah Bozian, Amex’s VP of agentic partnerships and strategy, described the rationale to TechCrunch as pulling intent earlier into the transaction flow so that risk is assessed before a charge lands rather than after. Her illustrative example: a customer instructs an agent to buy white Nike trainers in a size nine, the agent attempts to purchase Adidas instead, and Amex can block the transaction at the point of credential validation.

The framework extends commitments Amex made in April when it launched its ACE developer kit and Agent Purchase Protection, under which eligible cardholders who authorise an agent and pass authenticated intent to Amex would be protected from charges caused by agent error. The April release described that protection as a future commitment with terms still to be finalised, and two of the kit’s five services remained in development at that point.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Amex can move quickly here because it operates a closed-loop model as issuer, network and acquirer simultaneously, giving it end-to-end visibility over a transaction that a four-party scheme cannot replicate without coordination across multiple counterparties. That same four-party challenge is being addressed at an industry level through EMVCo‘s draft Intent Services framework, whose public comment window closed on 30 September, and through a voluntary principles paper published last month by a group of six global banks including Bank of America.

The direction of travel across all three workstreams is consistent: liability will follow whoever holds an authenticated, signed record of what the customer actually authorised. That creates an immediate practical question for issuers and processors operating on Visa and Mastercard rails. Any bank or processor whose agent partners cannot capture, cryptographically sign and pass intent data through the authorisation chain will find itself in a weaker dispute position as agentic transactions scale.

The regulatory frame is still forming. Neither the FCA nor the Payment Systems Regulator has yet issued specific guidance on AI agent transactions, though the PSR’s existing authorised push payment fraud reimbursement rules place significant weight on whether a payer gave genuine, informed consent. An authenticated intent record of the kind Amex describes would be a compelling artefact in that context. European regulators working through PSD3 implementation will face the same definitional question: at what point does an agent’s action constitute the customer’s consent?

For merchants, a payment credential scoped to a specific intent represents a meaningfully stronger dispute position than a stored card number submitted by an automated process. The commercial incentive to accept intent-scoped credentials is real, and acquirers will need to decide how quickly they build the acceptance infrastructure.

title: Payward to Acquire Saldo Bank in EU Banking Licence Push
snippet: The Kraken parent's deal for the Lithuanian specialist bank would add deposit, lending and SEPA capabilities across five European markets, subject to regulatory approval. The post Payward to Acquire Saldo Bank in EU Banking Licence Push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Payward, Inc., the unified financial infrastructure group that operates Kraken and a portfolio of trading and asset-management products, has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Saldo Finance Oy, the Finnish holding company whose subsidiary Saldo Bank UAB holds a banking licence granted by the European Central Bank and regulated by the Bank of Lithuania.

The deal is subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close in 2027. Financial terms were not disclosed.

What Saldo brings to the table

Saldo Bank currently serves customers in Lithuania, Finland, Sweden and Germany, with a passport to operate in the Netherlands. Its product suite includes retail term deposits across all four active markets, consumer loans in Lithuania, Finland and Sweden, and secured and unsecured SME loans in Lithuania and Finland. A credit card is live in Finland and is scheduled to launch in Sweden next year. The bank also provides embedded lending infrastructure to other fintech firms operating in Finland and Germany, making it a B2B player as well as a direct-to-consumer lender. At the end of September 2026, the bank employed just over 90 people.

For Payward, the acquisition extends a licensing stack it has been assembling over several years. The group already holds a Federal Reserve limited-purpose master account in the United States and an e-money institution licence granted by the Central Bank of Ireland. An EU banking licence is a material step up: it unlocks deposit-taking, card issuance, lending and full SEPA payment rails under a single regulated entity, with passporting as the mechanism for cross-border scale.

Co-chief executive Arjun Sethi was direct about the commercial logic. “A regulated EU bank is the piece that lets us serve European clients the way a primary financial institution should: one place to hold assets, move them freely, and put them to work,” he said. “We believe whoever owns that relationship earns the right to serve everything around it.”

Payward Banking, the banking pillar of the wider group, has already originated more than two billion dollars in loans. The Saldo acquisition is designed to bring that lending capability into the European regulatory perimeter, alongside yield-bearing deposits and banking-as-a-service functionality for third-party fintech clients.

Regulatory and competitive read-across

The transaction sits inside a broader pattern of crypto-adjacent infrastructure groups seeking full banking status in the EU. Holding a banking licence rather than an EMI licence matters for several reasons: deposit-guarantee scheme membership, the ability to pay interest on deposits, and access to central bank liquidity facilities. It also brings tighter capital requirements under the Capital Requirements Regulation and direct supervisory oversight from the ECB, which adds compliance overhead but confers credibility with institutional clients and corporate treasurers.

The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, which reached its final implementation phase this year, has sharpened the commercial value of regulated banking infrastructure for digital-asset firms. MiCA creates a clear authorisation pathway for crypto-asset service providers, but it does not grant deposit-taking or lending powers. A bank licence does. For Payward, which already trades under the Kraken brand with a significant European retail and institutional client base, combining MiCA-authorised crypto services with a licensed bank gives it a more complete financial institution proposition than most peers can currently assemble.

Competitors in the space, including several neobanks and banking-as-a-service platforms with EU licences, have generally grown the bank-to-crypto direction rather than the crypto-to-bank direction Payward is taking. Whether the regulator-to-regulator transfer of supervisory confidence is straightforward will depend on how the Bank of Lithuania and ECB view the change of control and the acquirer’s compliance framework. The 2027 close timeline suggests Payward is not expecting a quick approval.

The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering.

  

            						

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'

In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.

Notes to editors

The FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: What New Research Tells us About why Women in Fintech Hold Back
snippet: New research suggests stereotypes and vague promotion criteria contribute to the confidence gap in fintech, highlighting how women and employers can make career progression more transparent. The post What New Research Tells us About why Women in Fintech Hold Back appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A little while ago, I was having a mentoring session with a young woman working in fintech. She’s ambitious, and she’s been building her career in the industry for several years.

At some point in our conversation, she mentioned something almost in passing. She’d decided not to apply for a role she’d been interested in. A role we’d actually discussed a couple of weeks earlier.

Naturally, I asked her why. She told me she’d gone through the job specification and counted how many of the boxes she ticked. While she ticked quite a few, she didn’t tick all of them.

So, she’d made a decision. She wasn’t ready.

Here was a capable, experienced woman who was interested in progressing her career and, rather than putting herself forward and letting someone else decide whether she was right for the role, she’d ruled herself out.

So, I asked her a question. “How many of those boxes do you think the last person in that role ticked?” She couldn’t tell me. Honestly, neither could I. But I’d have been willing to bet that they didn’t tick every single one.

This isn’t new. I’m sure we’ve all seen the stat that gets regurgitated on LinkedIn every couple of months about how most women apply for jobs only when they meet 100% of the qualifications, whereas with men, that number’s around 60%. We call it a confidence gap.

New research published this year may offer a different way of understanding why this happens.

What the research says

This year, a new piece of research on the confidence gap really stuck with me.

It came from Harvard Business School‘s Katherine Coffman, who has spent years studying how stereotypes shape the way women see themselves.

She found that even when men and women have the same qualifications, women are less likely to apply for promotions and that a big part of that confidence gap comes from stereotypes.

We tend to think of stereotypes as something other people hold about us. Her point is that they shape what we believe about ourselves, too. If the industry around you has spent decades signalling that finance is a man’s game, it’s not a huge surprise if some of that seeps in, even when your track record says otherwise.

The gap gets wider when the criteria are vague.

When the rules are clear, women are more likely to go for it. When they’re not, though, the stereotypes creep into the gaps, and women rule themselves out,

By vague, I mean a job ad that asks for strong commercial acumen or senior presence, for instance. Or, a promotion that depends on being ready for the next level, although nobody has clarified what the next level involves.

Essentially, if you’re left guessing what the employer wants, or whether you qualify, it’s likely the vague language Coffman is referring to.

How to fix the confidence-gap in fintech

I’ve been careful to put both tips for women, and fintech employers, as I don’t believe this should be left for women alone to fix.

There are, of course, things we can all do to challenge the way we see ourselves. However, if the environment around us continues to reinforce the very behaviours we’re trying to unlearn, we’re only addressing half the problem.

So here’s what I think can be done on both ends.

For women in fintech

1. Write your own criteria down

If vague criteria are where self-doubt creeps in, the most useful thing you can do is take the vagueness away yourself.

I like to do this, and it’s hugely helped with any imposter syndrome I’ve had over the years.

Instead of measuring yourself against a spec that someone’s likely rushed through, or used AI to help draft, you should measure yourself against your own accomplishments and the brilliant things you’ve achieved since starting your career in fintech.

You can do this by making a comprehensive list that you continue to build on after each significant milestone. This could be the banking relationships you’ve opened, the volumes you’ve helped to move, the markets you’ve launched in, or the audits you’ve got through.

Be sure to put numbers and metrics next to each achievement. That way, when you’re weighing up an opportunity, you can check it against that list rather than the voice in your head.

2. Don’t underestimate your worth and what you bring to the table

This one’s for anyone who advises, consults, freelances or negotiates their own package or salary. Decide what your expertise is worth before the conversation starts, not halfway through it when the other person goes quiet, and you panic.

I work in high-risk payments and banking, and I know how valuable the work I do is. It’s the difference between a business getting banked and being able to operate, or not being able to trade at all.

It’s very easy to price the work you do as if you’re doing someone a small favour. So work out the value of the outcome and write your number down. When you’ve said it, let the silence sit. Silence isn’t a no.

3. Apply anyway

While this may sound like a no brainer to a lot of you, I feel I’d be remiss not to include it in this op-ed.

Job specifications are of course important because they tell you the skills and requirements needed and the ideal candidate for the role.

But, it’s important to remember that they’re just essentially wish lists and, a lot of the time you don’t necessarily need to have every single skill on them to still be considered.

So, and I mean this wholeheartedly, if the role excites you and you feel that you can do the majority of what they’re asking for, apply.

The worst that can happen is that they turn you down. Which, in my opinion, is always better information to have than the a no that you gave yourself.

For fintech founders

1. Make “ready” visible

If you run a fintech, write your promotion requirements down and share them. All of them, in plain English. This way everyone will have a clearer understanding of what’s needed to be promoted and what you’re looking for.

What does a compliance analyst actually need to have done to become a manager? I don’t mean vague niceties, but what exact proficiencies and experience? What does being ready for the next level actually look like in practice, at your company, this year?

Coffman points to Progress software as a good example here. The company realised its employees, particularly women, were struggling to work out how to advance. So it mapped out clear promotion pathways and made the expectations transparent, and it saw lot of improvements in both development and retention of its employees.

2. Name the gap when it matters

There’s been another study that came out this year that found something really interesting. It was by … and essentially shows that telling women about the confidence-gap can change their behaviour.

The caveat here, though, is when you tell them. Because the timing really is important apparently. The research suggests that the best timing is the exact moment when they’re thinking about applying.

To do this, you need to be sharing information about the gap in your job ads and bringing it up to employees in performance reviews or when you’re looking to hire internally.

Tell the women on your team, directly, that the research says they’re less likely to put themselves forward for this role, and that you’d really like them to.

A little encouragement goes a long way.

Final Thoughts

As for the woman I mentioned at the start, she applied. I don’t know yet whether she’ll get the role, and I’ll be gutted for her if she doesn’t. But the research is pretty clear that the applying is the bit that matters, and she’s already done the hard part.

We’ve spent so many years telling women that they need to be more confident and I just don’t think that’s done much. Maybe, moving forward, we need to be showing them the rules instead.

title: The B2B payment stack wasn’t built for how businesses pay now
snippet: The B2B payment decision used to be binary. Legacy infrastructure still is.
fullText:
In 2024, ACH overtook checks  as the most common form of B2B payment in the U.S, but it took more than a century to get there. The Federal Reserve centralized check clearing around 1920. ACH came online in 1972 and spent 50 years catching up.

In the last decade alone, there’s been an exponential increase in payment modalities. Consumer payments gained Venmo, Zelle, Apple Pay, Cash App and tap-to-pay. B2B followed with its own set of new rails, each one adding a different set of fraud controls, settlement timing, remittance expectations and compliance rules. 

A single B2B relationship today might involve ACH, virtual card and check, all routing to different payees through different systems. For complex industries like healthcare and property and casualty, that mix shows up every day: one claim payout can route to a provider as ACH, a member as a prepaid card, and a contractor as a check, all off the same adjudication decision.

The payment mix is modern. The infrastructure moving it wasn’t built for how businesses pay now.

The decision set has expanded. Legacy infrastructure hasn’t. 

For most of the last century, the B2B payment decision was binary: check or ACH. 

Today, the decision set is vastly wider. ACH, real-time payments, virtual card, cross-border, embedded. Each with different fraud profiles, settlement timing, remittance expectations and compliance frameworks. Legacy infrastructure wasn’t built for any of them.

“The paper check problem” only makes it worse. When a legacy infrastructure can’t handle a modern payment type natively, the workaround carries its own cost: a separate vendor, manual process and parallel system someone has to maintain. This combined processing, postage and labor push the true cost of a check to $4, compared to $0.26–$0.50 for an ACH transaction. 

Fraud only compounds the problem further. In 2025, 76% of organizations were hit by payments fraud. Every new payment type an organization adds opens a new fraud vector that legacy controls weren’t built to catch.

Continuing to run modern payments on legacy infrastructure may seem like a cautious move, but it’s the riskier position, and it costs more the longer it stays.

Payments under pressure. 

The shift from checks to ACH is more than a one-year headline. Between 2015 and 2024, ACH’s share of B2B payments climbed from 25% to 41%, while check share fell from 32% to 13%.

The pressure is mounting, and it comes from the highest levels. In March 2025, the White House ordered federal agencies to stop issuing paper checks. The Treasury made the case in one line: checks are 16 times more likely to be lost, stolen or altered than a digital payment, and the paper infrastructure cost the federal government $657 million in FY2024. If the federal government can’t justify keeping checks, why should anyone else?

Regulation is closing in on the digital side, too. NACHA’s new rules for risk management, effective March 20, 2026, require real-time fraud prevention and detection on all outbound ACH payments. This now makes fraud prevention and security a required capability for payment infrastructure.  

Organizations face two infrastructure demands at once: meeting regulatory requirements for digital payments and responding to policy pressure to move away from paper. Legacy systems were not designed for those demands, making modernization harder to defer.

What legacy infrastructure can’t handle at scale 

Legacy B2B infrastructure was built around point-to-point payment flows rather than the full lifecycle, and this fragmented reality shows up in operations. In AP, a supplier calls about an invoice stuck in approval for 45 days; a controller discovers three vendor records point to the same TIN. In healthcare claims, a provider calls because a check for a resolved claim never arrived; the exception queue holds 200 items of unapplied payments and unposted remittances. 

Different industries, same breakdown: the people approving the payment and the people moving the money are working in different systems, with different vendors and the handoff between them is where cost accumulates.

That same handoff is where fraud finds its opening. BEC, vendor impersonation, bank account change attacks: each one targets the handoff between where a payment is decided and where the money moves. Legacy infrastructure wasn’t built to protect this blind spot, and modern fraud is sophisticated enough to exploit it.

What a modern B2B payment platform does differently

The scale of the fragmentation is already measurable. More than 90% of organizations use two or more payment vendors to run their payment lifecycle. 30% use four or more, and 55% say their systems don’t talk to each other. Proving that consolidation isn’t aspirational. It’s the obvious fix to a problem businesses are already quantifying. 

A modern B2B payment platform does one thing legacy infrastructure can’t: it owns the payment from the moment it’s decided to the moment it’s reconciled. One system, every payment type, end-to-end.

Every modern payment option runs through the same integration, so adding real-time payments or virtual card doesn’t mean another vendor contract. The payment partner holds and controls the payee payment preference, so the payer’s workflow doesn’t change but the payee experience does. Remittance travels with the money instead of chasing it and fraud monitoring runs against the full transaction history. And because the platform integrates directly with the core systems where AP, treasury and claims operations teams already work, nothing gets re-entered and no one switches tools to move a payment forward.

ECHO built their core platform for this exact architecture: one integration, full lifecycle visibility, multi-layered fraud prevention and security, and direct integrations with the core systems where finance and claims operations teams already work.

Payments aren’t moving back to binary. That leaves one question: Is the infrastructure moving your payments built for where B2B is going, or where it’s been? 

To see how ECHO is building B2B payment infrastructure for the modern payment set, visit https://www.echohealthinc.com/.

title: Xero Connects Live Financial Data to Google Gemini for SMBs
snippet: Xero says it is the first financial management platform to launch a connected app for Gemini, giving small businesses real-time data access in conversational The post Xero Connects Live Financial Data to Google Gemini for SMBs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Xero has launched a connected app for Google Gemini, enabling small businesses, accountants and bookkeepers to query live financial data from within the Gemini interface. The integration, announced on 14 October 2026 from Wellington, allows users to retrieve profit and loss statements, check cash positions, surface overdue invoices and generate visual reports through conversational prompts, without leaving the Gemini environment.

Diya Jolly, president of product and technology at Xero

The capability is powered by JAX, Xero’s agentic platform, which maintains a secure, continuously synchronised link between a user’s Xero instance and the Gemini session. Xero confirmed that financial data shared between platforms is used solely within the active session and is not used to train Google’s models, a data governance commitment the company is describing as foundational to the integration.

Diya Jolly, president of product and technology at Xero, said: “Connecting Xero financial data into Gemini conversations helps small businesses and their accountants and bookkeepers instantly check their financial position, track cash flow and manage invoices and bills, all without breaking their workflow.”

What the integration does

The current release covers five functional areas: financial health reporting, sales and receivables tracking, payables management, interactive visual chart generation, and contact and organisation data retrieval. A forthcoming Gemini Tasks feature, described as coming soon for eligible plan tiers, will allow users to build time-based workflows that combine Xero data with other Google Workspace tools such as Gmail, for example automating follow-up sequences on overdue invoices or scheduling daily cash position summaries.

Xero has built a human oversight requirement into any action that modifies financial data. Issuing an invoice or sending a payment reminder requires explicit user confirmation before execution, a design choice the company frames under its “Accountable Intelligence” principle. That framing positions the platform as augmenting rather than replacing the accountant or bookkeeper’s judgement.

The Gemini integration extends a series of AI assistant connections Xero has launched in 2026, which already includes Microsoft 365, Anthropic‘s Claude, Claude for Small Business and ChatGPT. A new capability allowing accountants to switch between client organisations across all of these integrations without losing data context is also being introduced alongside the Gemini launch.

Market context

The race to embed accounting and financial management data into AI assistants reflects a broader shift in how software vendors are competing for SMB workflow time. Platforms that can anchor themselves as a trusted data layer inside tools professionals already use, whether that is Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or an LLM chat interface, reduce the daily friction of context switching and deepen switching costs at the same time.

Xero’s claim to be the first financial management platform to launch a connected app for Gemini is notable given the competitive pressure in cloud accounting. Rivals including Intuit’s QuickBooks and Sage also have active AI development programmes and their own integrations with major productivity suites. The pace at which Xero has connected to multiple LLM environments in a single year suggests that distribution through AI assistants is now a primary commercial priority, not an experimental add-on.

From a regulatory standpoint, the integration raises practical questions about data residency and audit trail integrity for accountants operating under professional standards obligations in the UK and EU. Xero’s session-only data commitment addresses the training-data concern directly, but advisors working under GDPR and ICAEW or FRC practice rules will still need to satisfy themselves that live financial data flowing into a third-party AI environment meets their client confidentiality requirements. Xero has not published a detailed technical data-flow document in the release.
